semblage of linked circles within a plane can be represented as the union of two closed curves that intersect at a single point.  This fact forms the basis for a key observation in our discussion, where we also note that any such assemblage of linked circles is associated with a unique non-crossing embedding of a triangle into the plane.  A "spine" of the triangle's edges can then be drawn to represent a two-dimensional structure that lies within the triangle, and this spine will be indicated by the triangle's vertices in order.  This method of representation allows us to assign a two-dimensional spine to each orientation of the assemblage of linked circles.  A particular type of function, which we call the "filling function," can then be defined for the assemblage when a specific circle is excluded.  This filling function will be a linear combination of the remaining circles' lengths, with coefficients that are the integers corresponding to the triangle's vertex ordering.  The assemblage's non-perturbative monodromy theorem can then be formulated as the statement that two assemblages of linked circles are topologically equivalent if and only if their filling functions are topologically equivalent when the circles are oriented in an arbitrary manner.  A related set of functions, which we call the "winding functions," can also be defined for the assemblage.  These winding functions will be linear combinations of the assemblage's circle lengths, with coefficients that are the Betti numbers of the assemblage's non-compact filling in the plane.  The non-perturbative monodromy theorem can be further expanded to include these winding functions, and it can be proven that two assemblages of linked circles are topologically equivalent if and only if their filling functions and winding functions are topologically equivalent when the circles are oriented in an arbitrary manner.  The non-perturbative monodromy theorem also provides the basis for a new type of invariant that can be defined for assemblages of linked circles with a non-trivial Betti number, and this invariant can be used to demonstrate the existence of distinct topologically equivalent graph link classes.  A graph link is defined as an assemblage of linked edges within a graph, and it is considered equivalent to another assemblage of linked edges if there exists a combination of edge reversals and node additions/removals that can transform the first assemblage into the second.   noisy speech without retraining.

We used high-resolution UV spectra from the $XMM-Newton$ satellite to analyze the physical conditions in the gas surrounding dormant black holes in local galaxies, with masses ranging from $10^6$ to $10^8$ M$\sun$. The study of 22 dormant low-mass AGNs with 80 detected narrow emission lines revealed the presence of an AGN-driven gas flow, likely associated with the "radio AGN fan sequence." The emission line analysis allowed us to investigate the physical properties of the gas, including its velocity, temperature, abundance of elements, and optical depth, and to explore the variability of these properties over time. The analysis indicated that the line ratios can be explained by a two-component gas structure, comprising a high-velocity, metal-poor component with a different abundance than the interstellar medium, and a slower, more abundant component. The study of the line profiles revealed the rotation curves of the galaxies, which correlated with the optical rotation curves, and the detection of the [Fe\,xvii] line at 18.79 \r{A} provided insights into the physical conditions of the gas, suggesting that the majority of the emission originates from photoionized gas rather than X-ray heated gas. The analysis also revealed variations in the line strengths and profiles over time, which we attribute to the perturbation of the gas flow by the supermassive black hole. The study demonstrates the value of high-resolution UV spectroscopy in investigating the physical conditions of the gas surrounding dormant black holes in local galaxies. The findings of this research can be applied to more distant galaxies, providing a complementary understanding to that gained from mid-IR spectroscopy, and the study paves the way for a deeper analysis of the variability of these galaxies using machine learning techniques. The comprehensive data products of this study are available for the detected emission lines, which we hope will benefit the scientific community and spur further research on this topic.   decay channels to the $0^+$ ground state and $2^+$ excited state of $^{32}$ 
  Ne, as well as the $J^{\pi}$ values and branching ratios for excited states 
  in the $^{32}$ Ar decay products.

The notion of a perfect matching cut is more restrictive than the conventional cut in a graph. The concept of a cut-dense graph arises from the opposite perspective, where every pair of vertices can be connected by a sequence of perfect matching cuts. We are tasked with identifying all pairs of vertices that cannot be connected to each other within a given tree-like structure, and we have the option to divide this tree into multiple subgraphs to achieve this goal. Our primary approach involves using cut-dense graphs as lookup tables to determine which pairs of vertices can or cannot be connected to each other. The way we divide the tree to create these subgraphs affects the size of the lookup table required. Our strategy is guided by the desire to minimize the number of subgraphs while maximizing the density of the lookup table. To this end, we introduce a new operation that combines multiple lookup tables in a specific way, and we show that this operation is valid based on the properties of cut-dense graphs. We also demonstrate how to create a set of pairwise distinct lookup tables that cannot be combined in this way, and these tables have the same structure as the one proposed in our algorithm. The size of this set is directly related to the number of pair-wise distances in the original tree-like structure, and it serves as an upper bound for our approach. To obtain this set, we generate all possible cut-dense graphs of a given tree-like structure, and we do this by applying a set of rules to these graphs. , the concept of spacetime is postulated to be absolute, thereby rejecting the possibility of physical observers being at rest within it.  This paper demonstrates that, contrary to prevailing understanding, the postulate of spacetime absoluteness is not a fundamental principle, but rather an derivable consequence from the invariance of physical laws under all possible Lorentz transformations.  The proof involves showing that absolute spacetime results from postulating the symmetry of space and time rather than their separation, and that this implication holds true under the condition that physical laws remain unchanged for all observers.  The paper also explores the related concept of general relativity, revealing that Einstein's gravitational theory arises from combining the principle of spacetime absoluteness with the postulate of inertia maintenance in the absence of external forces.  The paper further reveals that this combination leads to the curvature of spacetime and, consequently, geodesic motion.  However, it also becomes clear that the term "curved spacetime" is, in fact, misleading because it suggests the existence of spacetime as a pre-existing entity that can be curved, rather than deriving the geometry of the spacetime from the properties of the existing fundamental entities, namely mass and energy.  The paper ultimately shows that the term "curved spacetime" is a metaphor that should be used with caution to describe the outcome of gravitational interaction, rather than the interaction itself.  The paper also presents a critical assessment of the concept of curved spacetime in relation to the theory of general relativity, detailing the historical development of this concept, the role of mathematical tools in uncovering its implications, and the difficulties encountered in interpreting the physical meaning of this concept.  The paper concludes by highlighting the challenges of the "metric field" approach in providing a clear physical explanation for the curvature of spacetime, and explores the alternative approach of geodesic motion derived directly from the fundamental laws of physics, namely Newton's second law and the invariance of physical laws under Lorentz transformations.  The paper also discusses the concept of the gravitational field as a force responsible for the curvature of spacetime, and examines the related issue of the relationship between the gravitational field and the curvature of spacetime in order to clarify the physical meaning of this relationship.  The paper further presents a key insight into the nature of the gravitational field, namely that it is a result of the interaction between the spacetime geometry and the mass and energy present in it, and explores the implications of this insight on the physical meaning of the curvature of spacetime

  In the standard model, this is achieved by assigning different phases to the neutrino
  mass matrix's diagonalizing unitary matrix.  However, the physical phase present
  in the complex conjugate of the neutrino mass matrix's diagonalizing unitary matrix
  is difficult to measure directly.  Instead, its value can be inferred from oscillation
  experiments and lepton colliders.  This study examines the physical phase in the
  complex conjugate of the neutrino mass matrix's diagonalizing unitary matrix,
  denoted as $\delta$, which is associated with the phenomenon of CP violation.
  First, we review the methods for determining $\delta$'s value, starting from
  its initial estimation in 1998 to the present day.  Then, we discuss the primary
  methods for measuring $\delta$ in both neutrino oscillation experiments and lepton
  colliders.  We predict that the value of $\delta$ can be accurately measured for
  the first time in experiments at the Future Circular Collider (FCC).  We also
  calculate the sensitivity of various current and future experiments to $\delta$'s
  value, which is currently estimated to be able to measure $\delta$ to an error
  of 0.05-0.07 radians in the near future.  We conclude by discussing the potential
  for lepton colliders to complement neutrino oscillation experiments and the FCC in
  measuring $\delta$ and to achieve an error of 0.01 radians in measuring $\delta$'s
  value.  We also examine the compliance of various colliders with the required energy
  needed to accurately measure $\delta$ and the characteristics of the most promising
  colliders' physics cases.  Finally, we outline the planned or proposed experiments
  and the necessary upgrades required to achieve an error of 0.01 radians in measuring
  $\delta$ and the potential ways to achieve this with the current generation
  experiments.  We also touch upon the future directions of research related to $\delta$.
  We review the interconnection between $\delta$ and the CP phase in the kaon system,
  the status of the current understanding of the CP phase in the quark sector,
  the potential for lepton colliders to measure the CP phase in the quark sector,
  and the future prospects of research related to the CP phase in the quark sector,

The model also predicts the creation of domain walls in the universe during this phase, with wall densities falling within the range of 10^-7 to 10^-5, which could be identified through the observation of gravitational waves generated by these walls. We demonstrate that the solution remains close to the original trajectory when the strength of the perturbations is kept within certain bounds, specifically we show that there exists a probability greater than zero for which the solution stays near the original trajectory for an infinite duration. This finding is particularly significant in scenarios where initial conditions fluctuate randomly, as it indicates that there are probabilities greater than zero for which the solution will behave stably even when the density is unevenly distributed over an infinite period. This discovery also extends to scenarios with the presence of external forces and rotation within an infinite, unbounded domain. It's worth noting that our approach focuses on the stability of the stationary solution rather than the asymptotic behavior of the system. Additionally, under certain conditions on the initial density distribution, we found that the system will behave similarly to the corresponding homogeneous system. This research builds upon the work presented in [Cuip and Vela, 2014], where the stability of the Euler equation was analyzed with periodic boundary conditions in the presence of external forces and rotation within a finite, bounded domain. This finding can be applied to a broad range of scenarios, including conditions under which the system will behave similarly to a system with constant density, and there are illustrative examples provided in the study. Furthermore, we have also established the existence of probabilities greater than zero for the existence of infinite-time instabilities in the system, which can occur even when the density is evenly distributed, as seen in the model representing the behavior of the Eulerian system driven by forcing from a random field.   Mars Exploration Rover (MER) mission measured electric field variations in
  the atmosphere of Mars using a technique called floating potential detection.
  Analyzing pre-sunset local time data from 35 solar day periods at the
  Meridiani Planum site, the FPF data revealed a distinct pattern - a
  phenomenon with a peak magnitude of 1.5 volts and a duration of roughly 20
  minutes was observed during each day. This phenomenon was found to occur
  just before sunset and was attributed to a specific atmospheric process,
  which could be described as a dust vortex forming near the surface and
  releasing charged particles as it moves upwards. The discovery of this
  vortex could help explain previously observed patterns of atmospheric
  electricity on Mars and may also provide insights into the transport of
  particles and gases within the planet's atmosphere.  The vortex phenomenon
  was found to be most prevalent during the Martian spring and summer, and
  was observed to be restricted to the pre-sunset period, which is when the
  atmospheric pressure is highest, indicating that it may be driven by
  pressure gradients within the vortex. The study also found that the peak
  voltage occurred when the rover was oriented towards the sun, suggesting
  that the vortex may have a specific direction of movement. The researchers
  believe that the vortex may be a persistent feature of the Martian spring
  season and could be influenced by the temperature differences between the
  day and night surfaces, which may lead to the uplift of charged dust
  particles. The study's findings have implications for the understanding of
  atmospheric processes on Mars that could have influenced the environment
  of the MER rovers, as well as the habitability of the planet, and may
  also be relevant to the study of atmospheric electricity on other planets
  and moons with surface activity. The vortex was found to release a small
  amount of mass per second, which is comparable to a gentle breeze, and
  may be responsible for the dispersion of particles and chemicals within
  Martian soil. The study's results have been verified using models of the
  Martian atmosphere and a newly developed dust aerosol transport model.  A
  statistical analysis was performed to validate the model's results which
  involved using the FPF data to estimate the distribution of charged dust
  particles within the Martian atmosphere and testing this against actual
  measurements of the atmospheric electricity on Mars.

We develop a mathematical model to explore the competitive dynamics of two identical cell populations with slight differences in behavior. Our model incorporates a mechanistic representation of resource allocation and a game theory framework to capture the strategic interactions between cells. We apply our model to investigate two key aspects of coexistence: how small initial discrepancies develop into distinct populations, and how existing populations respond to a new, rival cell type. We use recent advancements in applied equilibrium dynamics to extend the equilibrium state approach, enabling us to analyze the statistics of a general forced dissipative system at equilibrium. This methodology enables us to derive specific insights into the structure and evolution of the Earth's climate system. Specifically, we find that the distribution of the system's natural modes can be understood using a simple scattering diagram, where the locations of the modes remain fixed but their oscillation amplitudes vary in response to changes in the system's geometry and forcing. This model, based on Dukes' theory, assumes that water's viscosity is resistant to changes in temperature and pressure because of these aligned molecules, which act as obstacles to flow. We further develop this model by incorporating the effects of temperature, pressure, and molecular alignment on viscosity, and test it against a comprehensive set of experimental data spanning a broad range of temperatures, pressures, and shear rates. Our results show that this model accurately predicts the viscosity of water across various conditions, which we find indicates non-Newtonian behavior. Furthermore, we extract key parameters from our model, using which we simulate the viscosity of water at different temperatures and pressures without the need for actual experimental measurement. We also utilize our model to analyze the flow of water in two specific scenarios and predict the viscosity of water at depths where the pressure is extremely high, such as in deep-sea hydrothermal vents. A major bottleneck hindering the scalability is the costly neighborhood aggregation process, which involves repeating graph propagation steps until convergence or a stopping criterion is met. 

  To break through this limitation, we introduce a novel GNN architecture called DecoupledGraph, which separates the learning process into two distinct stages: an initial fast propagation phase and a slow converging phase with adjusted learning rates. 

  DecoupledGraph treats the aggregation process as comprising two decoupled components: one representing the underlying graph structure and another capturing the high-level representation of the input data. Previous studies have primarily focused on local level connections within the DMN, neglecting higher level abstract relationships that characterize its modular structure. Utilizing recently developed advanced brain mapping techniques from the Neurosympy package, our study employed an innovative analytical approach to extract the brain's functional connectivity components at both local and global levels of organization. We applied this method to analyze the default mode network in two separate datasets and discovered distinct components within the DMN, each with unique spatial patterns and combined effects that collectively reflect the entire default mode component. We further investigated the spatial distribution of these components and identified their correspondence to specific brain regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and temporal parietal cortex. Notably, our results demonstrated the default mode component's complex and multifaceted nature, comprising multiple sub-components that align with the proposed hierarchical taxonomy of the brain and its networks. To facilitate further research and exploration, we have made our findings openly available through an interactive data visualization tool, allowing users to delve into the intricate details of the default mode network's hierarchical organization. By using a phenomenological model for electron energy distribution, we calculate the emission spectra in different reconnection regimes - steady state, instantaneous, and averaged - and analyze the spectra's evolution throughout the reconnection process. Our model indicates that the synchrotron emission spectra can be described by a power-law with an exponential cutoff, where the energy index and the cutoff energy are both reconnection regime-dependent. Our simulations show that the overall energy index ranges from 0.3 to 1.7, the cutoff energy varies substantially, and the total synchrotron radiation energy can make up a significant portion of the magnetic field's initial energy. We find that the radiation energy peaks during the impulsive phase, while the total energy remains significant throughout the reconnection process. We also derive an expression linking the synchrotron radiation's characteristic energy to the magnetic field strength and reconnection rate, and demonstrate that the electron energy distribution can be described by a self-similar function of time. Our results suggest that magnetic reconnection can generate synchrotron radiation with an extremely broad spectral range, spanning from hard X-rays to sub-TeV gamma-rays. We further propose that the associated particle acceleration and light curves could be recognizable in future observations of X-ray and gamma-ray flashes. We make our simulation data publicly available, in the hope that they may serve as references for ongoing and future multi-wavelength observations of magnetic reconnection. We also emphasize the importance of simultaneous observations across different wavelengths to the understanding of magnetic reconnection's physical properties and the physics of extreme astrophysical events. We further note that the analysis of our simulated light curves can be applied to other contexts, such as supernova remnants and pulsar wind nebulae. We also highlight potential observational opportunities for the Square Kilometre Array and the Cherenkov Telescope Array in this area. We further propose that future simulations should be designed to account for the effects of radiation on electron acceleration and the associated photon regulation of particle acceleration. a simple experiment in which two participants make independent decisions about whether to cooperate or defect in a one-shot situation for their mutual benefit or individual gain. While this scenario has been extensively studied with complete information about participants' past actions, their intentions, and reactions to varying payoffs, a more common real-life experience involves strangers with no connection in a large population where individual actions have only a minimal impact on others. We conducted a large-scale experiment involving a hundred participants without prior knowledge of each other's actions or identities, multiple sessions with distinct rules, and a significant financial incentive. The results showed that approximately sixty percent of the time participants chose to cooperate, and a significant increase in cooperation was observed when anonymous feedback about the actions of others was provided. The data also revealed that each participant's future actions were largely determined by their initial action, and a significant portion of them demonstrated a tendency to stick to either cooperative or defective behavior across multiple sessions. We found that a simple model based on random choice effectively matched the observed patterns in the experiment, and a detailed analysis of its components helped identify the key factors influencing the decisions made by participants. The findings also showed that a similar model previously tested in a laboratory setting with complete information about participants' actions did not produce the same results, and a key factor revealed to be previously unknown is the tendency to stick to either cooperative or defective behavior. This phenomenon is associated with a level of confidence in either choice, and its implications are both theoretically and practically significant. The model was then used to predict the outcomes of various scenarios tested in the experiment, and the predicted results matched the actual findings. The paper concludes by discussing the novel insight into the prevalence of cooperation in anonymous societies and highlights the importance of distinguishing between initial and subsequent actions of the same individual. The paper also emphasizes the importance of using models that take into account the tendency to stick to either cooperative or defective behavior in predicting the outcomes of large-scale experiments with a significant financial incentive. Initially, we propose a 2D shape estimation algorithm called the Decoupled Parametric Shape Estimation (DPSE) framework, which uses minimalistic parametric models to estimate an object's shape.  The DPSE algorithm decouples model optimization from 2D surface rendering, leveraging two separate networks to achieve this.  The proposed method produces two output maps: one containing 2D surface coordinates and the other comprising weight maps for the parametric model.  Optimization occurs using these maps, which are generated automatically without the need for additional supervision.  We further develop a non-rigid object shape estimation task using single RGB-D images, introducing the Decoupled Sparse Surface Estimation (DSSSE) algorithm.  The DSSSE model optimizes a sparse surface representation for a non-rigid object, estimating both 3D surface coordinates and weight maps for surface rendering.  We tested the DPSE on the MIGNT dataset and the DSSSE on the IRA dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results in both cases.  We believe our method contributes meaningfully to the non-rigid object shape estimation community, suggesting potential applications for future work on 3D surface reconstruction techniques. However, these methods fail to account for the variable brightness of meteors, a critical factor that affects their detection and tracking. To address this limitation, we developed a hybrid model that combines a brightness-invariant optical flow technique with a logistic function to represent the probability of meteor existence. The model was tested on real data captured at the Avena Observatory in Spain, covering a year and a half of meteor recordings. The results showed that the hybrid model's accuracy compared to the current method is 86.5% for correct detections, 3.5% for false positives, and 9.0% for false negatives. To further evaluate the model's performance, we simulated observations with increasing background noise and found that the hybrid model's effectiveness decreases significantly when the signal-to-noise ratio drops below 10. Notably, the current method becomes less effective at this point, whereas the hybrid model requires a ratio of at least 20 for comparable results. To explore the impact of image resolution on meteor detection, we conducted experiments at the Avena Observatory with different camera apertures, finding that a maximum aperture of f/1.6 provides the optimal balance between brightness and image resolution. We demonstrate that this conjectured lower bound is achievable when the manifold's dimension is between 2 and 4, thereby establishing lower bounds for the first eigenvalue of the Dirac operator on these dimensional manifolds. Within these dimensional parameters, the proposed lower bound can be expressed as a function of the manifold's volume, and this bound is shown to be stringent for certain rotational manifolds. Moreover, we derive precise formulas for the first eigenvalue and total scalar curvature of these rotational manifolds with a dimension greater than 4. In particular, we examine a specific C^1 subdifferential polynomial and demonstrate that its derivative can be expressed as a sum of two convex functions with essentially finite generalized first moments, thereby gaining insights into the structure of these functions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these functions and the additive relation of their derivatives, which leads us to a key theorem stating that a C^2 function is convex if and only if both its first and second derivatives are convex and their sum over the real line has an essentially finite generalized second moment. This process is proven to be globally convergent if the initial function has a globally defined subdifferential and convex-related derivatives everywhere. Also, we establish the convergence of this process for a specific class of C^1 subdifferential polynomials, which can be characterized by the non-existence of certain polynomial roots.   are shared with a second student that generates the final translation. We tested
  our method on two datasets and the results show that it can effectively use

By applying a similarity transformation to the quark-glucson effective interaction, we obtain the effective glucson-glucson interaction within the nucleon. Through a glucson field expansion, we derive a effective glucson field theory where the nucleon is described as a three-body system of glucsons. By correlating the glucson field with the quark field, we establish a connection between the quark-glucson effective theory and the effective field theory approach. To our knowledge, we have developed a new set of effective glucson-glucson interactions within the nucleon, where the glucson is described as a nearly massless quark. We have also derived a new effective glucson field theory where the nucleon is described as a three-body system of glucsons. We have tested our approach by applying it to the calculation of the nucleon's mass and charge radius. We have found that our approach matches the existing results obtained through the quark-glucson effective theory approach. We have also obtained a new result for the chiral symmetry breaking parameter within the nucleon, which we have denoted as $\hat{\Sigma} \approx 1.34 GeV^2$. We have tested the consistency of our approach with the chiral perturbation theory at the quark level. We have also investigated the glucson content of the nucleon at the pion mass, which we have found to be less than 20%. As one of the most distant galaxies detected in HI observations, with evidence of an extensive, neutral gas reservoir, we believe that this discovery has important implications for our understanding of mass growth in galaxies at high redshifts.  As such, further investigation of this galaxy and its surrounding environment is warranted, and we propose that it be added to the observatory priorities for future deep surveys with radio telescopes.  With its currently estimated redshift of 0.934, we note that this galaxy will soon become accessible to a variety of new observatories in the near-infrared band, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, the Giant Magellan Telescope, and the Extremely Large Telescope, which will allow for a more in-depth analysis of its physical characteristics. This strategy, termed the 'neutral' option, refrains from using perturbative QCD to evolve the initial color glass condensate and instead utilizes a novel representation of gluon distribution functions. Based on a recent study, we demonstrate that the neutral evolution correctly yields the expected conformal properties of parton distributions. Additionally, we have conducted a detailed computation of conformal coefficients associated with the gluon distribution and found that they differ significantly from their vacuum counterparts. Our findings also imply that the neutral evolution leads to a non-trivial change in the functional form of the gluon distribution, particularly notable in the small-$x$ region. As a direct application of these results, we have incorporated the conformal properties into a new model of parton distributions within the neutral evolution framework. Our research has further explored the impact of different non-linear effects on the evolution of parton distributions. We have also examined the effect of the initial glue-to-quark density ratio on the evolution of parton distributions and found that it influences the behavior of the gluon distribution in the large-$x$ region. Our research has also focused on the neutral evolution of the gluon distribution within a quark-diquark model of proton structure. As a concrete example, we have used our model to make predictions about deep-inelastic scattering off a nuclear target and found that the neutral evolution leads to a softer than expected $A^{\frac{1}{3}}$ dependence in the large-$x$ region. number of dimensions 'd': given a linear flow in 'd' dimensions with a time component, determine the number of invariant principles it possesses that are symmetries of the Minkowski metric.  Our findings indicate that there are 'd' linearly independent invariant principles for 'd' dimensions, although this is not the case when 'd' exceeds two.  In addition, we demonstrate the invariance of the Minkowski metric to specific linear flows in two and three dimensions, which are not necessarily symmetries when 'd' is greater than two.  Our research also explores the relationship between these invariant principles and the concept of Killing vectors.  We provide the exact methods for determining the invariant principles of linear flows in any number of dimensions and detail the underlying geometric principles that define these structures.  Our work includes explicit examples of the invariant principles for two and three dimensions.  We further analyze three-dimensional spacetime and find that the majority of linear flows possess only one invariant principle, although there are exceptions, such as the Bautista-Araya gauge flow, which has multiple invariant principles but still has only 'd' dimensions when 'd' is two.  Our discoveries also highlight the challenging nature of the problem when 'd' exceeds two.  We hope that our research contributes to a better comprehension of linearly expanding spacetimes and the underlying geometric principles that define these structures.  We also propose the term'spacetime symmetries of expansion' (SSE) to describe the invariant principles of linear flows and believe that this concept is novel.  We also introduce the term'spacetime symmetry of expansion vector' (SEV) to refer to the vector that defines these symmetries.  Our research indicates that the SSE can be determined from the Einstein field equations when the spacetime has a maximally symmetric expansion but this is not the case when the spacetime is not symmetric.  We also propose the term'spacetime symmetry of expansion tensor' (SET) to describe the tensor that defines the spacetime symmetries of expansion in a compact form.  Our research also explores the relationship between the SSE and the conformal Galilean symmetry of expansion (CGSE) and finds that they are equivalent when the spacetime has a maximally symmetric expansion but this is not the case when the spacetime is not symmetric.  We also propose the term 'conformal Galilean algebra of expansion' (CGAE) to describe the algebra that defines the CGSE.

  insights into Electroweak Sector properties and allows for the extraction of $W^0$ self-energy

  measurement for $pp \to W^0 \gamma \gamma \to \mu^-\mu^+ \gamma \gamma$ is calculated to be 5.6 fb^-1 at 95%
  confidence level for a 3.2 GeV threshold on the invariant $\mu^-\mu^+ \gamma \gamma$ mass and 2.8 fb^-1 at
  95% confidence level for a 5.0 GeV threshold on the invariant $\mu^-\mu^+ \gamma \gamma$ mass. This research
  also explores ways to optimize cross-section measurements by exploring various kinematic selections and
  reconstruction techniques, and examines the purity of $W^0\gamma\gamma$ candidates by investigating background
  processes and evaluating the consistency of measured cross-sections with quantum field theory predictions.  A
  case is made for further, more sensitive $W^0\gamma\gamma$ production experiments at the LHC, and it is shown
  that a 300 fb^-1 data set at 13 TeV would allow for the extraction of $W^0$ self-energy components with
  precision on the order of 20% or better.  A simulation-based study indicates that a threshold of 2 GeV on the

(Mageac) experiment was an
  atmospheric Cherenkov imaging array that conducted deep air shower research
  between 2003 and 2005 off the coast of Brazil. Mageac's unique location near
  sea level allowed it to study the low-energy end of the cosmic ray spectrum.
  Although the experiment had a relatively short operational period of one
  year, its data revealed several significant findings, including an interpretation
  of the Knee feature in the cosmic ray energy spectrum and a related calculation
  of the average depth of air shower maximum. In addition, Mageac's data helped
  constrain existing simulations of air showers and led to the development of a
  new method for determining the depth of air shower maximum. The experiment's
  analysis also yielded important insights into the properties of very high-energy
  cosmic rays, particularly those in the 10^18 eV to 10^19 eV range, and its
  findings align with various theoretical models, including acceleration mechanisms
  in magnetic fields and the effects of cosmic microwave background on cosmic
  rays. The Mageac team's analytical approach is also applicable to future
  experiments at high-altitude sites. Unfortunately, the team was unable to
  further analyze the data due to limitations in simulation tools available at
  the time, but with the introduction of SimAirShower, a new code capable of
  accurately simulating air showers at depths less than 10 units of mean free
  path, the team was able to reexamine the data and gain new insights into the
  properties of very high-energy cosmic rays. The code's results confirm several
  key features in the cosmic ray energy spectrum and provide a physical
  interpretation of the Knee feature, and it also reveals the importance of
  hadronuclear interactions in the production of air showers, particularly those
  with energies above 10^18 eV, and it leads to a new calculation of the average
  depth of air shower maximum, which is more accurate than previous estimates

  experiments, and it also results in a new formula for the expected depth of
  air shower maximum based on the energy and the maximum altitude of the
  primary particle, and it indicates that the depth of air shower maximum is
  generally greater than 200 g/cm^2
